extracted.intended_audience: organizers of academic research workshops (AIM-style), especially in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running AIM-style online research workshops that replicate the collaborative outcomes of in-person workshops, with practical notes on format, tools, and constraints. Focuses on enabling new problems, new collaborations, and sustained follow-up work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should begin work on new problems, with new collaborators, and the work should continue long after the week of the workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as AIM's primary metric for success for all AIM-style workshops. Design choices should be evaluated by whether they help achieve these outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize significant small-group work time
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is facilitated by significant time for work in small groups, supported by a few lectures and large group discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop schedules should prioritize blocks for small-group problem work; lectures and whole-group discussion are supportive rather than dominant activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule must accommodate time zones
rubrics_metrics.description: The format and schedule of an online workshop must take into account the realities of time zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning synchronous sessions, consider participant time differences to avoid excluding contributors; staggered or repeated sessions may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for participants' unavoidable commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: The format and schedule of an online workshop must take into account people's unavoidable commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that attendees cannot be fully dedicated as in-person; build flexibility into timing and session length so participants with other responsibilities can contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for a variety of technology and user experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The format and schedule must take into account the variety of technology and experience using that technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tools and workflows that are accessible to participants with differing levels of technical comfort and varying hardware/connectivity; provide simple onboarding and fallback options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of virtual social activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities, like hanging out at happy hour, are beyond current technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some informal, serendipitous interactions are hard to reproduce online; plan alternative ways to foster informal contact but be realistic about limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative experimentation and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Online AIM-style workshops will continually improve over time through experimentation, evaluation, and iteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat design choices as hypotheses to test; collect feedback and refine formats across successive workshops rather than expecting a single perfect design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use presence/space platform to track people and activities (Sococo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sococo provides the infrastructure for keeping track of people and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a virtual 'space' to represent rooms and help participants find others and activities; Sococo (or similar) can create the feeling of place and support transitions between small groups and lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use threaded group chat for asynchronous organization (Zulip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zulip, a threaded group chat platform, is particularly helpful for organizing collaborative work that is taking place asynchronously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a persistent, threaded chat tool to coordinate ongoing group work, share resources, and continue collaborations outside synchronous sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spatialized social tools for informal interaction (Gather.town)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather.town is a video-game-like interface that simulates being at a large party where you can see who is there, but you can only talk with the people in your immediate vicinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Gather.town-style tools to enable proximity-based, casual interactions and to approximate the social dynamics of in-person gatherings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across collaboration sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: AIM also uses Sococo for smaller collaborations, such as SQuaREs, and larger collaborations, such as AIM Research Communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen formats and tools should scale: the approach should support both small working groups and larger community events, with appropriate adjustments to structure and tooling.
